rules.message: Async Express/router handler with no surrounding try/catch, `next(err)`, or `.catch()` — on Express 4, an unhandled rejection in an async handler crashes or hangs the process; Express 5 forwards async rejections to error-handling middleware automatically, so there it's a style/consistency concern rather than a crash bug. A route wrapped by error-handling middleware like `express-async-handler` or `express-async-errors` is also safe, but that wrapping isn't visible in the handler body this rule scans — the rule's biggest real-world false-positive source. Wrap in try/catch and call `next(err)`, or attach `.catch(next)`.

Synchronous fs/child_process call (`readFileSync`, `execSync`, etc.) alongside request-handler evidence (a `req.`/`request.` member access, or a response-API call like `res.status(...)`/`res.send(...)` — deliberately NOT `res.json(`/`res.text(`, which a fetch `Response` also has, so a handler whose only response evidence is a bare `res.json(x)` is accepted as a miss rather than risking fetch-response false positives) — a blocking call on the request path stalls Node's event loop for every concurrent request. Use the async `fs.promises`/`child_process` APIs, or move CPU-heavy work to a worker thread.

`.map(async ...)` used without wrapping the result in `Promise.all`/`Promise.allSettled` — `.map` returns pending Promises, so a rejection becomes unhandled and any ordering/completion guarantee is lost. IF ANY CODE CONSUMES THE RESOLVED ARRAY, DO NOT SWAP IN `Promise.allSettled(...)`: it resolves to settlement wrappers (`{ status, value }` / `{ status, reason }`) rather than to the values themselves, so every downstream reader gets a wrapper where it expected a record. Whether anything catches that depends on the consumer, and the compiler is the good case — an array that flows into an annotated field fails to build, while the swap is silent exactly where the value is `any`, untyped, or merely spread into a log line or a response body. Wrap the call in `Promise.all(...)` (or `Promise.allSettled(...)` for expected partial failures).

Debug flag or disabled TLS verification (`debug: true`, `NODE_TLS_REJECT_UNAUTHORIZED=0`, `rejectUnauthorized: false`) committed to source — ships a dev backdoor or TLS bypass to production if deployed unchanged. The two TLS shapes are Node-specific, but the `debug: true` shape is not, and this rule scans Rust as well: a struct literal (`Settings { debug: true }`) fires exactly as a JS object literal does. Remove the flag, or gate it behind an environment check in whichever language the line is written in — `process.env.NODE_ENV !== 'production'` in Node, `std::env::var` in Rust. Suppress a vetted line with `// zzop-debug-true-committed-ok`.

`Promise.all(...)` used with DB write calls on a DB-client-shaped receiver (`prisma`/`db`/`tx`/`client`/`repo`) — non-atomic: some writes land and others don't when one rejects, with no rollback for what committed. Co-occurrence heuristic, not proof — it flags a `Promise.all(...)` and a write call in the same function, not that the writes are actually inside the `Promise.all(...)` array; confirm that before acting, because the anchor line is often a `Promise.all(...)` that awaits no write at all. THE REMEDY TURNS ON WHAT HAPPENS TO THE RESOLVED ARRAY, AND ONE BRANCH SILENTLY CHANGES ITS VALUE. IF THE RESOLVED ARRAY IS DISCARDED (the call is awaited for its effects only), use `Promise.allSettled(...)` and add compensation logic for the entries that rejected. IF ANY CODE CONSUMES THE RESOLVED ARRAY, DO NOT SWAP IN `Promise.allSettled(...)`: it resolves to settlement wrappers (`{ status, value }` / `{ status, reason }`) rather than to the values themselves, so every downstream reader gets a wrapper where it expected a record. Whether anything catches that depends on the consumer, and the compiler is the good case — an array that flows into an annotated field fails to build, while the swap is silent exactly where the value is `any`, untyped, or merely spread into a log line or a response body. Wrap the writes in one transaction instead, or unwrap at every consumer (`r.status === 'fulfilled' ? r.value : ...`) before the value is used. THE CLAUSE ABOVE DESCRIBES A GATE THIS RULE DOES NOT IMPLEMENT — nothing here proves that the writes sit inside the `Promise.all(...)` array — AND THE `info` SEVERITY IS THAT ABSENCE MADE MACHINE-READABLE RATHER THAN LEFT IN PROSE. The band is advisory rather than a build-breaking signal, and it stays `info` until that gate is BUILT rather than described.

`JSON.parse(...)` called directly on apparent external input (`req`/`body`/`params`/`query`/`payload`/`event`) without a surrounding `try` — malformed input throws, turning a bad request into a 500 or a process crash. WHEN THIS FINDING IS WRONG: a local `try` is not the only catcher. A framework-level async error boundary — Express 5's, or an `asyncHandler`-style wrapper around this handler — turns the same throw into a proper response with no `try` on this line, and this rule reads only the surrounding lexical block. The external-input judgment is a NAME match as well: a local named `payload` that never left the process looks the same as a request body. Wrap the parse in try/catch and return a proper 4xx on failure.

Outbound HTTP call (`fetch`/`axios`/`got`) in server/worker code with no timeout or `AbortController` visible in the same function — `fetch` has no default timeout, so a hung upstream hangs the request and can exhaust the connection pool. A timeout set on a shared client instance in another file (e.g. `axios.create({ timeout })` in a helper module) isn't visible to this per-function check — this is the rule's biggest real-world false-positive vector. SCOPE IS DECIDED PER FILE BEFORE ANY FUNCTION IS READ: only a file carrying a server/worker signal is scanned at all — a framework import (`express`/`fastify`/`koa`/`hono`/`@nestjs`), a receiver-qualified `http.createServer(`/`net.createServer(`, a numeric `.listen(`, a Workers binding or a `.prepare(` call — so a Node entry point that calls a bare `createServer(` imported from `node:http`, or any file that borrows its server object from a helper module, is never looked at and its missing deadline is never reported. The receiver on `createServer(` is required on purpose: bare `createServer(` is also what `miragejs` and Vite's dev server are called, and without it this rule reads a frontend mock-server file as backend code. A DEADLINE TURNS A SLOW SUCCESS INTO A FAILURE, AND THE ABORT ONLY REACHES THIS SIDE OF THE WIRE: the peer never hears it, so a call that times out may already have been received and acted on — the charge made, the row written, the mail sent — and this side cannot tell that from a request that never arrived. Size the value against what this particular call does rather than a round number, since an upload, a report query or a cold start legitimately outlasts an interactive request; and where the call is not idempotent, give it an idempotency key or a reconciliation path in the same change, because a retry past a timeout is a second attempt at work that may already be done. Pass an explicit timeout (e.g. `AbortSignal.timeout(...)`) or wire up an `AbortController`.

A `reqwest` HTTP client is constructed inside this function (`Client::new()` / `Client::builder()` / `Client::default()` / `ClientBuilder::new()`, or the `reqwest::get(url)` convenience call — which builds a fresh, timeout-less default client on every invocation — in a file that names `reqwest` at all) and no `.timeout(` call appears in the same function body — reqwest's default client has no request timeout, so a peer that accepts the connection and then stalls holds this task, its connection and whatever it borrows for as long as the peer likes. Scope, disclosed rather than assumed: the veto is FUNCTION-LOCAL, purely lexical, and matches the METHOD spellings `.timeout(` and `.read_timeout(` only — so a client built by a shared constructor elsewhere and merely used here is invisible to it, a timeout configured outside this function reads as absent, and a caller-side deadline such as `tokio::time::timeout(...)` does not clear it either (use the suppression marker for that case) — confirm before changing code. `read_timeout` DOES clear it: it bounds exactly the stalled-peer read this message describes. `connect_timeout` deliberately does NOT clear it: that caps the HANDSHAKE only, and the stalled-peer failure above begins after the handshake succeeds. A DEADLINE TURNS A SLOW SUCCESS INTO A FAILURE, AND THE ABORT ONLY REACHES THIS SIDE OF THE WIRE: the peer never hears it, so a call that times out may already have been received and acted on — the charge made, the row written, the mail sent — and this side cannot tell that from a request that never arrived. Size the value against what this particular call does rather than a round number, since an upload, a report query or a cold start legitimately outlasts an interactive request; and where the call is not idempotent, give it an idempotency key or a reconciliation path in the same change, because a retry past a timeout is a second attempt at work that may already be done. Set one: `Client::builder().timeout(Duration::from_secs(5)).build()`, or `.timeout(..)` on the individual request builder; for `reqwest::get` there is no builder to put one on — construct a client instead. The TypeScript sibling is `reliability/fetch-no-timeout`.

Body parser (`express.json`/`urlencoded`, `bodyParser.json`/`urlencoded`) configured without an explicit `limit` — the code relies on the implicit 100kb default, which is too small for some legitimate endpoints and simply unexamined for the rest. WHERE the limit may sit, stated because this rule reads lines rather than syntax: the same line as the call, or the line immediately after it — which is where a formatter puts it when it wraps the options object (`express.json({` / `  limit: ...`). That second spelling was invisible to this rule until 2026-08-21, and it was not a corner case: across directus and 38 corpus trees the trigger appeared 33 times and a same-line `limit:` matched 0 of them, so the one tree that had actually taken this advice was the one tree that got flagged for it. RESIDUAL, and it is a contract rather than an oversight: exactly one line in each direction. A limit written two or more lines below the call — after another option, say — still reports, and the fix there is the suppression marker `// zzop-body-limit-missing-ok` rather than a rule change, because widening the reach into a span would make how-far-to-look a per-rule setting and an unbounded walk is how a veto starts silencing genuine findings elsewhere in the same function. Set an explicit `limit` (e.g. `{ limit: '1mb' }`) sized to the endpoint's needs.

`setInterval(...)` with no matching `clearInterval(...)` anywhere in this file — a leaked timer keeps the process (or page) alive and re-fires forever, since nothing cancels it. WHEN THIS FINDING IS WRONG: the search is FILE-SCOPED, so an interval whose handle is exported, returned, or handed to a caller that clears it in another file is indistinguishable from a leak here. And a process-lifetime interval — a daemon heartbeat, a metrics flush meant to run until exit — has no teardown to attach to; there the honest close is a suppression marker, not a `clearInterval` nobody calls. Store the return value in a handle and call `clearInterval(handle)` during teardown/cleanup.

A file/stream handle (`fs.createReadStream(`/`fs.createWriteStream(`/`fs.open(`/`fs.openSync(`) is opened structurally inside a loop body — verified against the parser's projected loop spans (the open call's own line falls within a loop statement's or array-iteration callback's span), not merely co-occurring with loop syntax somewhere in the same function — and the enclosing function never closes it (`.close(`/`.destroy(`/`pipeline(`/`finished(` anywhere in the function). Under a fan-out, the file descriptors accumulate across iterations and the process eventually hits `EMFILE: too many open files`. Note honestly: the close-absence check is whole-function scoped and matches `.close(`/`.destroy(`/`pipeline(`/`finished(` on ANY object — so a close inside a sibling branch or a callee is invisible here and the finding still fires (false positive), while an unrelated `res.close()`/`conn.destroy()` elsewhere in the function vetoes a genuine stream leak (false negative); verify before refactoring. Close the handle in a `finally` block, or use `pipeline(...)`, which closes both ends automatically.

An EventEmitter listener (`.on('event',…)`/`.once(`/`.addListener(`/`.prependListener(`, anchored on a string event-name argument) is registered structurally inside a loop body — verified against the parser's projected loop spans (the subscribe call's own line falls within a loop statement's or array-iteration callback's span), not merely co-occurring with loop syntax somewhere in the same function — with no matching removal (`.off(`/`.removeListener(`/`.removeAllListeners(`) anywhere in the enclosing function. To avoid firing on same-shaped non-EventEmitter `.on('...')` calls (a frontend DOM/jQuery `$(el).on('click', …)`, a knex join builder, a D3 selection), the rule only scans files that use a Node event-emitter/server library (an `events`/`net`/`http`/`ws`/`socket.io`/... import, or a `.setMaxListeners(` call). This is the event-listener sibling of `interval-no-clear` (which covers `setInterval`): listeners pile up on every iteration, Node warns `MaxListenersExceeded`, and each event then fires the handler N times (duplicate side effects, unbounded memory growth). Note honestly: the removal-absence check is whole-function scoped — a teardown living in a different function (or an unrelated `.off(` on another object) either misses a real fix or vetoes a real leak; verify before refactoring. Register the listener once outside the loop, or collect the listeners and remove them during teardown.

`await` used directly inside a `Promise.all(...)`/`Promise.allSettled(...)`/`Promise.race(...)` array literal — each awaited element resolves before the next element of the array is even evaluated, so the calls run one after another instead of concurrently, silently defeating the whole point of `Promise.all`. This is syntax-proven where it fires: an `await` textually between the array's `[` and `]` on the SAME line always serializes that element against the next (the line-scan only sees the single-line form — a multi-line array with each `await` on its own line is not flagged). Move the `await` out — build the array of un-awaited promises first, then await the combinator once (e.g. `Promise.all([getA(), getB()])`, or `await Promise.all(items.map((i) => getA(i)))`).

An `async` callback registered as an EventEmitter listener (`.on`/`.once`/`.addListener`/`.prependListener`) — the emitter fires it and discards the returned promise, so a rejection inside the handler becomes an unhandled promise rejection, which crashes the process on Node 15+ (and is a silent swallow on older Node). The rule only scans files that use a Node event-emitter/server library (an `events`/`net`/`http`/`ws`/... import, or a `.setMaxListeners(` call), so a frontend DOM `el.on('click', async …)` is not flagged. Wrap the handler body in try/catch and log/handle the error there, or wrap the callback so its promise is observed (e.g. a small `catchAsync(fn)` helper).

A create/write call (`fs.writeFile`/`fs.open`/`fs.rename`/...) appears LEXICALLY AFTER a filesystem existence/permission check (`fs.existsSync`/`fs.access`/`fs.stat`/...) in the NEAREST enclosing function, with no exclusive-create flag (`wx`/`O_EXCL`) visible anywhere in it — CWE-367 TOCTOU: between the check and the use, the path can be swapped out from under it (e.g. via a symlink) or another writer can win the race, so the check is stale by the time the write happens. A trigger line that sits inside NO parser-projected function span (a class-property initializer, a top-level statement) is read as ungated, and the pairing there widens back to the whole scanned symbol span. The order is TEXTUAL, and path identity is not checked at all: it does not confirm the check and the write target the same path, nor that both run on the same control-flow path (`fs.existsSync(a)` followed by `fs.writeFile(b)` still fires). SAME-LINE NESTING RESIDUAL (a disclosed false negative shared by every rule that uses this order gate): on a single line "after" is decided by MATCH START OFFSET, so a check nested INSIDE the write call's own argument list reads as coming AFTER it and does not pair — `fs.writeFileSync(p, data, { flag: fs.existsSync(p) ? 'a' : 'w' });` is silently NOT reported, while the ordinary one-liner `if (!fs.existsSync(p)) fs.writeFileSync(p, data);` (check first) fires. Prefer opening with an exclusive-create flag (`{ flag: 'wx' }` in Node, `O_EXCL` at the syscall level), which fails atomically if the path already exists instead of trusting a separate check.

An `await`ed Node `fs`/`fs.promises` call (`readFile`/`writeFile`/`appendFile`/`unlink`/`rename`/`copyFile`/`mkdir`/`rm`/`readdir`/`stat`/`access`/... — deliberately excluding `open`/`createReadStream`/`createWriteStream`, which `stream-open-no-close-in-loop` already covers for the handle-leak angle) executes structurally inside a loop body — verified against the parser's projected loop spans (the call's own line falls within a loop statement's or array-iteration callback's span), not merely co-occurring with loop syntax somewhere in the same function — with no `Promise.all`/`Promise.allSettled` anywhere in the enclosing function. Each iteration's disk I/O waits for the previous one to finish before starting, serializing work the filesystem would otherwise run concurrently; over many files this adds up to iteration-count times the single-call latency. This generalizes `map-async-no-promise-all` (which only catches the `.map(async ...)` callback shape) to the ordinary `for`/`for-of`/`for-in`/`while` loop forms, scoped to `fs` I/O specifically — database calls in a loop are `sql/nplus1`'s territory and outbound network calls are `reliability/api-in-loop`'s, both already covering their own receivers, so this rule only anchors on an `fs`/`fsPromises`/`fsp`/`fs.promises`-shaped receiver to stay out of their way. Gather the paths up front and run the calls concurrently with `Promise.all(...)` (bounded by a concurrency limiter if the fan-out is large), or use a single directory-level/batch operation where the API allows it. Suppress a vetted case (e.g. deliberately sequential writes to preserve on-disk ordering) with `// zzop-fs-in-loop-serial-ok`.

A `go func(){...}()`/`go someCall(...)` statement is started structurally inside a loop body — verified against the parser's projected loop spans (the `go` statement's own line falls within a `for` statement's span), not merely co-occurring with loop syntax somewhere in the same function. ONE FINDING PER ENCLOSING FUNCTION, not per `go` statement: the finding anchors on the FIRST qualifying `go` line in the function body and no later qualifying `go` in that same body gets a line of its own, so `data.triggerLines` — how many lines of this function carry a `go` that passed the span check — is the only place the real count lives, and a value above 1 means this one function starts that many unbounded goroutines while only the first is named here. Fans out one goroutine per iteration with no bound: a large `range`/count exhausts memory or file descriptors long before the loop finishes. Before Go 1.22, every goroutine launched this way also captured the SAME loop variable (all iterations sharing one underlying variable, not a per-iteration copy), so most already ran with the wrong value by the time they executed. Bound the concurrency with a worker pool or a semaphore (`chan struct{}`/`golang.org/x/sync/semaphore`/`errgroup.SetLimit`), or, on pre-1.22 toolchains, copy the loop variable into a new local before passing it into the goroutine.

Network call made structurally inside a for/for-of/for-in/while/do-while statement or an Array forEach/map/filter/reduce callback — verified against the parser's projected loop spans (the call's line falls within a loop statement's span, or within an array-iteration callback's own span), not merely co-occurring with loop syntax somewhere in the same function — so it fires one request per iteration, the HTTP analogue of N+1 (rate-limit / serial-latency risk). Batch via a bulk endpoint, or gather inputs and issue one request (or a bounded Promise.all). A file with no projected loop spans is silently skipped by this rule — for the `.ts`/`.tsx` files this rule scans, that realistically means a degraded parse (oversized file or syntax failure), the same graceful-degrade policy method-scan already applies to missing symbol spans.

A `setX(...)` state setter call appears LEXICALLY AFTER an async boundary (an `await`, or a `.then(`/`.catch(`/`.finally(` continuation) in the same function body, with no unmount/abort guard (`AbortController`/`AbortSignal`/`isMounted`/`mountedRef`/`signal:`/`cancelled`/`didCancel`) anywhere in that body — the reported line is the first setter that actually follows the boundary, not merely one that shares the function with it. THE GUARD VOCABULARY HAS TWO ARMS, and the second exists because the first is a hand-typed list of exact spellings and case-SENSITIVE: `cancelled` never matched `isCancelled`, the dominant React spelling, and a ref named `isDestroyed` was in no list at all (measured on getredash/redash @ ca79fe98: the second arm removed 12 of this rule's 35 findings there, every one a live guard with a cleanup, while that tree's one INERT guard kept reporting). The second arm is a SHAPE rather than a name: a flag whose identifier carries a cancel/abort/destroy/unmount/dispose stem, in any case, AND which is assigned `true` somewhere in the same body. A `stale` stem was in that list for one review cycle and was REMOVED, because a stem is a substring test and `stale` is cache-revalidation vocabulary rather than lifecycle vocabulary: an unrelated `let staleWhileRevalidate = true` inside the same effect silenced a genuinely unguarded setter (reproduced). The five that remain name teardown and nothing else. Demanding the assignment is what keeps the widening honest — a `let isCancelled = false` that nothing ever sets is an INERT guard (an effect returning no cleanup), the `if (!isCancelled)` wrapping the setter can never be false, and that finding is CORRECT and still fires, where a plain case-insensitive widening of the first arm would have silenced it. Two things the second arm still cannot do, stated rather than discovered: it does not prove WHERE the assignment happens, so a flag flipped on some non-cleanup path vetoes exactly as a cleanup does; and its stem list is still hand-written, so a project whose flag is named outside it (`bail`, `gone`) is not covered — those findings stay live rather than silently green, which is the direction a list of this kind should fail in. "Same function" means the NEAREST enclosing function, not the whole declaration: a boundary in a sibling closure no longer qualifies (measured on a 22-tree corpus: 6 of 87 findings changed — 4 dropped as sibling-closure or nested-callback pairings, 2 re-anchored onto a setter that genuinely follows a boundary in its own function), while a `.then(`/`.catch(`/`.finally(` continuation callback is scoped together with the call that schedules it, so a continuation setting state still fires. The flip side of that scoping: a setter inside a NESTED callback (a `.map`/`forEach`/`setTimeout`/event-handler closure) whose only boundary sits outside that callback no longer fires — an accepted under-report. The narrowing needs parser-projected function spans; a file whose spans could not be projected (parse failure, size cap, an external-parser envelope that omits them) keeps the old whole-declaration scope and its sibling-closure false positives. A trigger line that sits inside NO parser-projected function span (a class-property initializer, a top-level statement) is read as ungated, and the pairing there widens back to the whole scanned symbol span. This is a TEXTUAL ORDER claim, not a dataflow one: it does not prove the setter runs on the resumed continuation (a setter in an `else` branch still counts, and so does one that follows a CONDITIONAL boundary — `if (stale) { await refresh(); }` then `setX(...)` fires even on the path where nothing was awaited), and it does NOT prove the component can unmount while the request is in flight (a plain event handler is mounted by construction whenever it fires, so a `setX(...)` inside one is an accepted false positive here). THAT PARENTHESIS DESCRIBES A GATE THIS RULE DOES NOT IMPLEMENT, AND THE `info` SEVERITY IS THAT ABSENCE MADE MACHINE-READABLE RATHER THAN LEFT IN PROSE. The discriminator that would earn a `warning` is whether the setter sits inside a `useEffect` callback (or a function one calls) — the only shape where teardown can land between the request and its resolve — and that gate is NOT EXPRESSIBLE by this matcher: the projected facts carry function bodies as ANONYMOUS line spans with no record of which call receives a function as its argument, and the TypeScript producer deliberately leaves a `useEffect` callback UNMERGED from its call site (its one merge is for `.then`/`.catch`/`.finally`, and widening it would re-create the sibling-closure pairing that merge exists to break). Measured over a 9-tree corpus: 34 of 49 findings sit in an event handler rather than an effect — 31 of one monorepo's 45, and BOTH findings in the two React-17 trees, so a React-VERSION gate would have preserved nothing but false positives. Read this band as advisory: a list to review, not a signal to break a build on. It stays `info` until the effect-containment gate is BUILT rather than described. SAME-LINE NESTING RESIDUAL (a MEASURED false negative, disclosed rather than fixed): on a single line "after" is decided by MATCH START OFFSET, so an `await` nested INSIDE the setter call's own argument list reads as coming AFTER it and does not pair — `setData(await fetch(url));` is silently NOT reported, while the two-statement spelling (`const r = await fetch(url); setData(r);`) fires, same file, same run. This is the mirror image of the `p.then(r => setX(r))` one-liner that DOES fire (there the boundary token starts first); closing it would need structural nesting awareness that a start-offset comparison between two independent regexes cannot have. But when the setter genuinely follows an in-flight await inside code that CAN unmount mid-request (an effect's async loader, a callback stored across a lifecycle boundary), the resolve races teardown: a stale-data flash overwriting newer state, or a wasted render right after remount. THE HEADLINE SYMPTOM IS VERSION-BOUND AND THIS RULE DOES NOT READ YOUR REACT VERSION: the console warning "Can't perform a React state update on an unmounted component" was REMOVED in React 18.0.0, because the update was always a silent no-op and the wording read as a leak report it never was. There is no memory leak on any version — below 18 the residual cost is that console line, at 18 and above it is wasted render work only. Thread an `AbortController` (or an `isMounted`/`mountedRef` flag) through the async function and skip the `setX(...)` call if the request was aborted or the component has unmounted. The `require_file` gate scopes this to React files (a `useEffect`/`useState` call, or a `from 'react'` import) to keep it out of non-component async helpers. The `setX(` trigger is anchored to a bare (non-member) call so a `localStorage.setItem`/`res.setHeader`/`date.setHours` is not mistaken for a state setter, and `setTimeout`/`setInterval`/`setImmediate` are vetoed — so a genuine `setX(...)` that merely coexists with a timer in the same function is an accepted under-report.
